title: Revealed: UK relied on £2bn of ‘questionable accounting’ to hit its climate-aid goal - Carbon Brief
gist: Carbon Brief finds about £2.1bn of the UK's £12.8bn climate finance came from relabelling existing funding (MDB core funding, humanitarian aid, BII), without which the UK would have missed its £11.6bn target by about £924m; the practice is likely to make up about a third of the new £6bn target.

insights.claim: Around £2.1bn, nearly a fifth, of the UK's £12.8bn climate finance came from accounting changes rather than new spending; without them cumulative finance would be about £10.7bn, leaving a £924m shortfall against the £11.6bn target.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: The headline target was met only by relabelling; real additional money fell short.
insights.locator: '£1bn shortfall'

insights.claim: The £2.1bn figure is higher than the £1.7bn of reclassified climate finance that the Independent Commission for Aid Impact forecast in 2024.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Reclassification has exceeded official forecasts, suggesting further drift is possible.
insights.locator: This final figure of £2.1bn

insights.claim: The UK government has announced it met the £11.6bn target but has not released the full details or even the total amount provided by 2025-26.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Disclosure gap; independent FOI analysis is the only route to the real numbers.
insights.locator: The UK government has announced that it met

insights.claim: Total UK climate finance reached £12.8bn over five years, with a record £4bn in the past year.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Records a peak that the next period is set to fall away from.
insights.locator: '£1bn shortfall'

themes.theme: How the target was kept while aid shrank

insights.claim: To keep the £11.6bn pledge while cutting foreign aid, the Conservative government loosened the definition of climate spending in 2023, allowing existing funds to be relabelled; the Labour government has maintained this approach while cutting aid further.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Bipartisan accounting approach means the pattern will persist into the next target period.
insights.locator: In order to retain the target while cutting aid

insights.claim: The UK pledged the £11.6bn in 2019 as a doubling of its previous five-year target, but successive governments have slashed foreign aid, citing economic strain and the need for more defence spending.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Defence-spending priorities are crowding out aid and climate finance.
insights.locator: Since then, successive governments have slashed

insights.claim: The UK has set a new climate-finance target of £6bn over three years, making it one of the only major donors to set a post-2025 target, but this halves annual spending from £4bn to about £2bn on average.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Even the leading donor target implies a large annual drop; weak signal for the global scale-up toward $300bn by 2035.
insights.locator: The government has pledged £6bn of foreign aid

insights.claim: Continued use of questionable accounting is likely to make up around a third of the new £6bn target, according to previous Carbon Brief analysis.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Real new money in the next period may be nearer £4bn.
insights.locator: Previous Carbon Brief analysis also shows

insights.claim: Developed countries are obliged under UN treaties to provide 'new and additional' climate finance and have goals to mobilise $100bn a year through 2025 and at least $300bn by 2035.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Frames the benchmark that reclassification undermines.
insights.locator: The UK and other developed countries are obliged

insights.claim: Counting a share of core funding for multilateral development banks as climate finance adds £1.1bn, mainly via the World Bank and African Development Bank, making it the largest accounting change.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: MDB core funding is the largest lever the UK is using to inflate climate totals.
insights.locator: The first is counting a share of 'core' funding

insights.claim: MDBs face criticism for poor transparency on climate finance and reliance on loans rather than grants, while nearly all UK climate finance so far has been grant-based.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Counting MDB funding changes the grant/loan composition of reported climate finance.
insights.locator: However, MDBs have also faced criticism

insights.claim: The Trump administration has pressured multilateral banks to drop climate plans and has already forced the World Bank to abandon its target to put 45% of funds toward climate finance, reducing the predictability of flows from banks the UK is counting.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: US pressure undermines the premise for counting MDB core funding as climate finance.
insights.locator: Moreover, the US has been pressuring MDBs

insights.claim: Automatically counting 30% of humanitarian aid as climate finance for countries judged most climate-vulnerable contributes nearly £600m, including to Afghanistan, Sudan and the DRC, even for projects with no discernible climate link such as helping conflict-affected people in Yemen and orphans in Zimbabwe.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: The second-largest change is the most clearly decoupled from climate outcomes, a reputational risk.
insights.locator: The second-largest UK accounting change

insights.claim: The Center for Global Development has called the 30% humanitarian aid revision 'arbitrary', since every aid project is already screened for climate-relevant components.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Think-tank critique reinforces the credibility problem.
insights.locator: The Center for Global Development (CGD)

insights.claim: Calculating the climate share of BII investments from real investments rather than a default 30% added £133m over the first four years, and an internal forecast put the total change at £266m over five years.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: The BII change is small but data on it are inconsistent.
insights.locator: The third significant portion

insights.claim: BII has shifted toward clean power, reaching more than £1bn in climate investments in 2025, but has faced criticism for legacy fossil-fuel investments that conflict with UK priorities and for channelling aid to billionaires.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: BII is a key vehicle for clean-energy EM investment but carries reputational risk.

insights.claim: The UK also counted £99m of 'spending on COP26' as climate aid retrospectively.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Another example of retrospective reclassification.
insights.locator: There was also some extra spending

insights.claim: The International Development Committee concluded that, together with aid cuts, the UK's accounting changes have 'eroded' the 'additionality and credibility' of its climate finance.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Parliamentary scrutiny increases political risk for the accounting approach.
insights.locator: A recent International Development Committee (IDC) report

insights.claim: IDC chair Sarah Champion said the government has been cutting corners to maintain headline climate-spending commitments rather than delivering genuine climate and nature outcomes.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Signals possible pushback if next-phase targets lean on the same accounting.
insights.quote: the government has been cutting corners to maintain headline climate-spending commitments, rather than working to deliver genuine climate and nature outcomes
insights.locator: Responding to Carbon Brief's findings

insights.claim: The UK government says its accounting changes are consistent with internationally agreed ways of calculating ICF used by other major donors, and that it is proud to have hit and exceeded its third international climate-finance target.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: The official defence is that the approach is within international norms, so reform is unlikely without outside pressure.

insights.claim: The UK was traditionally viewed as taking a more rigorous approach to climate-finance accounting, which is notoriously unregulated and opaque.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: If even a historically rigorous donor relabels aid, other donors' reported totals are probably less reliable.
